channel.title: NewsCenter — Top 5 news of the day — 2026-11-09
channel.description: The five news that matter most today, chosen from Laurent's newsletters. 39 news received.

item.title: 1. American voters reject data center projects
item.description: Why it matters: Voter opposition to data centers signals a growing infrastructure and permitting constraint that could raise costs and slow AI expansion. In Alhambra, California, 83% of voters supported banning data centers, while in Wells, Maine, 82% approved a 180-day pause. OpenAI now proposes paying for electricity and infrastructure, publishing more information, and investing locally to win residents’ support.

item.title: 2. OpenAI launches GPT-6 Cyber to research vulnerabilities
item.description: Why it matters: OpenAI’s launch of GPT-6 Cyber marks a significant advance in AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and raises new cybersecurity and misuse concerns. OpenAI has launched GPT-6 Cyber, a restricted model capable of finding software vulnerabilities and building exploits for authorized security testers.

item.title: 3. Employers turn against AI at work after being overwhelmed by mediocre content
item.description: Why it matters: Employers’ backlash against mediocre AI-generated content could slow workplace adoption and shift demand toward higher-quality, human-supervised AI use. The campaign against AI-generated content in the workplace now has a powerful ally. Executives liked AI at work until they were overwhelmed by mediocre content.

item.title: 4. Google announces new AI controls for schools
item.description: Why it matters: Google’s new AI controls for schools could shape how education systems balance access to productivity tools with concerns about AI governance and classroom use. Google announced new school-related AI controls, raising the question of whether schools will be able to keep Search while rejecting its AI features.

item.title: 5. A gut-bacteria treatment reduces infections
item.description: Why it matters: A gut-bacteria treatment that sharply reduced infections in high-risk transplant patients shows promising clinical potential, though larger trials are still needed. In a small randomized trial, the cultured gut-bacteria treatment SER-155 reduced bloodstream infections in blood cancer patients receiving stem-cell transplants. Infections affected 10% of treated patients versus 42.9% of those receiving a placebo, but larger trials are needed.
